Measuring the kernel

Source: vignettes/articles/measurements.Rmd
measurements.Rmd
library(zutable)

Beneath the bracket, zutable groups, sorts, joins and reduces with a kernel of its own, written in C and usable from R through grp(), key_order(), key_sort(), grp_join(), grp_match() and grp_reduce(). This article is for readers deciding whether to call those functions directly, or wondering what the bracket costs. It says how the kernel was measured, where it is ahead and where it is behind, and what each number means.

A number is kept only when the answers agree

A benchmark that times two programs giving different answers measures nothing. So the harness reduces every result to a canonical form, such as the sorted sizes of the groups, and compares it across every tool before it keeps a time. Here is that rule on one row, at 10^6 rows instead of the record’s 10^7:

set.seed(1)
x <- sample.int(1e5, 1e6, replace = TRUE)
canon <- function(id) sort(tabulate(match(id, unique(id))))
results <- list(
  zutable  = grp(x)$id,
  collapse = collapse::GRP(x, sort = FALSE)$group.id,
  base     = match(x, unique(x))
)
vapply(results, function(id) identical(canon(id), canon(results$base)), NA)
#>  zutable collapse     base 
#>     TRUE     TRUE     TRUE

All three found the same groups, so their times may be compared. The first appearance order is the same too: grp(x)$id is match(x, unique(x)), which is the contract of grp().

identical(grp(x)$id, match(x, unique(x)))
#> [1] TRUE

The harness also records the settings each tool was given (one thread for data.table, collapse and DuckDB) and the peak memory of each call.

The record

tools/run-benchmarks in the package’s repository ran on 2026-11-19 on one x86-64 machine (Intel Core i5-8500B, macOS, R 4.6.2), one thread, 10^7 rows, median of five, with collapse 2.1.8, data.table 1.18.6.1, kit 0.0.21, vctrs 0.7.3, bit64 4.8.6, stringi 1.8.9 and DuckDB 2.0.0. The ratio is the other tool’s time over the kernel’s, so above 1 the kernel is faster. These are a selection of the targets the design set before any kernel code existed.

Operation Kernel (s) Other (s) Ratio
groups, one integer key, 10^3 distinct, against kit 0.170 0.163 0.96x
groups, one integer key, 10^3 distinct, against collapse 0.170 0.086 0.51x
groups, two integer keys, against collapse 0.515 0.273 0.53x
groups, symbol and hour of a skewed market-data day, against DuckDB 0.747 0.734 0.98x
order, integer, against base radix 0.237 0.337 1.42x
order, double, against base radix 0.495 0.378 0.76x
order, integer, against data.table 0.237 0.910 3.8x
order of 100 values, 10^5 times, against base order() 0.722 2.359 3.3x
order, reversed input, against base radix 0.093 0.379 4.1x
order, character, all distinct, against base radix 4.877 6.926 1.42x
order, character, 10^5 distinct, against base radix 1.895 0.336 0.18x
collated sort, 10^6 words, against stringi 0.096 1.100 11.5x
collated sort, 10^6 words, against base sort() 0.096 4.008 42x
inner join, one key, against data.table 1.012 1.603 1.58x
inner join, two keys, against data.table 1.059 1.351 1.28x
match, one key, against base match() 0.957 0.493 0.52x
sum, 10^5 groups, against collapse 0.062 0.023 0.37x
sum, 10^5 groups, against base rowsum() 0.062 1.692 27x
within-group deviation, against collapse 0.178 0.192 1.08x

What the numbers say

The kernel is ahead of base R wherever base has no specialised path: many small sorts, reversed input, collation, rowsum(), and joins through merge(). It is level with DuckDB, run at one thread, on the market-data shape, and ahead of data.table’s one-key join and its numeric order. It is behind collapse and kit nearly everywhere they compete, by 1.1x to 4.5x, and its peak memory is above the design’s budget for groups and joins, and above base radix’s for sorting.

Three choices explain much of the gap, and each is deliberate:

  • Sums are base R’s, bit for bit. The kernel accumulates in long double, as base sum() and mean() do, so grp_reduce() and the bracket’s aggregates give exactly base R’s answer. collapse sums in double. On x86-64 the long double adds cost 2.3 times as much when the groups fit in cache.
  • Groups keep first appearance. grp() numbers groups in the order they first appear and returns their sizes, starts and row order as well, whether or not the caller uses them.
  • Character keys sort in byte order by hashing. Base R’s radix sort orders strings through scratch space inside R’s string cache, which a package cannot use; the kernel groups the strings first, which costs more when they repeat.

The rest is tuning not yet done: the release was measured, not tuned.

Reading a number

Each figure is a median of five runs on one machine, so the ratios, not the seconds, carry over to another machine. Memory is the peak of R’s heap during a call, which counts everything the kernel allocates but misses what other packages take from malloc(). Above 10^7 rows, or for queries that need many operators at once, an engine such as DuckDB is the better tool, and the bracket’s plan is designed to be handed to one.
